narrative: Your promotion was denied because the model estimates a 67% probability that you will leave your job—meaning, based on your profile, leaving is judged more likely than staying. This assessment did not use your gender, age, or health information. The strongest signal pushing toward leaving was your total work experience of 6–10 years; among employees predicted to stay, half have only 1–5 years, so your longer overall experience raised the leave risk. The second strongest factor, having no other job opportunities, worked in your favor and pushed toward staying—most employees predicted to stay also reported no other opportunities—but it was not enough to offset the other signals. Third, your 1–5 years with your current organization pushed toward leaving; although this tenure is common among stayers, in your overall profile it added to the concern. Because these drivers are about career stage and tenure rather than proven job performance, you should ask for a clear conversation about promotion criteria, development opportunities, recognition, job stability, and retention plans. The organization should also consider whether predicted-leave risk should be decisive on its own, and discuss retention before denying promotion.
